primer.text: A book on a desk and a tug-of-war rope tell one story in two halves: sometimes the forces cancel, sometimes they leave a surplus. This note names the two cases, then turns the surplus into the most used equation in mechanics — force equals mass times acceleration.

modules.title: Balanced and unbalanced forces
modules.opening: Forces on one object combine along each line into a single resultant. When that resultant is zero the forces are balanced and nothing about the motion changes; when a surplus survives, the forces are unbalanced and the object must accelerate. This lesson fixes both words with the two standard scenes.
keyPoints: Balanced forces cancel completely, so the resultant force on the body is zero.
A book on a desk shows the standard balance: its weight downward against the desk's upward push.
Unbalanced forces leave a resultant, and that resultant causes the object to accelerate.
The acceleration may show as speeding up, slowing down, or changing direction.
A tug-of-war with 80 N against 100 N leaves a 20 N resultant towards the stronger side.

low.restatement: Cancel completely — balanced, nothing changes. Leave a surplus — unbalanced, and the surplus accelerates the object.
low.analogy: Two shopkeepers haggling over one till: equal pulls hold the till still; the stronger pull walks away with it.
low.examPointer: 'Balanced' questions want the phrase 'resultant force is zero' — not merely 'the forces are equal'.

medium.restatement: Balance is a statement about the resultant, not about stillness: a balanced object keeps whatever velocity it had, while any non-zero resultant rewrites that velocity.
medium.analogy: A barge in steady current: matched tow ropes hold its heading; one extra metre of rope on a side swings it — velocity responds to the surplus, not to the pull.
medium.examPointer: Direction of the acceleration follows the resultant's direction — state both when a question asks for the motion.

modules.title: The relationship F = m × a
modules.opening: One equation runs this whole note: the resultant force equals the mass times the acceleration. This lesson fixes the equation, its units, and the proportionality habits it rewards — doubling force doubles acceleration, doubling mass halves it — then applies all three in worked numbers.
keyPoints: The relationship is force = mass × acceleration, written F = m × a, also known as Newton's second law.
F is the resultant force in newtons, m the mass in kilograms, a the acceleration in metres per second squared.
For a fixed mass, doubling the resultant force doubles the acceleration.
For a fixed force, doubling the mass halves the acceleration.
A negative F value records a force acting opposite to the motion — a decelerating force.

low.restatement: Push harder on the same mass and it speeds up faster; push the same on a heavier mass and it speeds up more slowly.
low.analogy: Supermarket trolleys: an empty trolley leaps away at the same shove; the half-full one needs double the shove for the same getaway.
low.examPointer: Always check the units before substituting: kilograms and metres per second squared feed newtons directly.

medium.restatement: F = m × a is a proportionality law, not just a formula: a scales with F for fixed m and with 1/m for fixed F — the two habits behind most rearrangement questions.
medium.analogy: It behaves like a see-saw: force and mass at the ends, acceleration the tilt — load one end double and the tilt answers in kind.
medium.examPointer: When a question hands you a negative force, say why: the minus sign marks a force opposing the motion, exactly the crash-test deceleration case.

glossary.definition: Describes forces whose combination leaves a non-zero resultant on the body.
The unit of force: 1 N accelerates 1 kg at 1 m/s².
The rate of change of velocity, in metres per second squared.
The law that the resultant force equals mass times acceleration, F = m × a.

workedExample.prompt: A car of mass 900 kg accelerates from rest to 27 m/s in 3 s. Calculate (a) the acceleration and (b) the force producing it.
steps: List the known quantities: initial velocity 0 m/s, final velocity 27 m/s, time 3 s, mass 900 kg.
The acceleration is the velocity change over time: a = (27 − 0)/3.
Newton's second law then gives F = m × a = 900 × 9.
